task.decision_user: An airline network planner or airport route-development analyst at the end of a new route's first month of reported operation, deciding whether to keep, up-gauge, or begin winding down the commitment (gates, slots, crew base, co-op marketing).

task.outcome_horizon: 12 to 14 months after the entry month (three-month anniversary window).
task.population: Eligible unit is one carrier by directed origin city market by directed destination city market entry episode. In month M the carrier reports Class F scheduled passenger/cargo service, total Passengers greater than zero and total DepPerformed at least 8, and the same carrier performed zero departures on that directed pair in every month M-12 through M-1. Both endpoints are U.S. airports or territories in the U.S. carriers domestic T-100 table. The carrier is a U.S. certificated reporting carrier identified by UniqueCarrier. Months M+12 through M+14 must exist in the downloaded panel. Only entry months inside the frozen train eval and holdout windows are kept; no outcome condition enters eligibility. Rows lacking a fully reported anniversary window are omitted as unknown labels, never relabeled negative.
task.prediction_time: Ninety days after the end of entry month M, after the monthly T-100 compilation for M is assumed available. Only T-100 records for months at or before M may enter features; months after M are unseen.
task.question: When a U.S. certificated carrier starts scheduled passenger nonstop service on a domestic city market pair it has not served in the previous 12 months, will that service still be operating in the anniversary quarter 12-14 months later?
task.simple_references: Majority-class control predicts still operating for every entry. Calendar-and-identity control uses carrier crossed with entry calendar month. Persistence analogue uses only the carrier trailing-12-month route-attrition rate plus carrier size as a single-feature score. Hub-presence rule predicts survival whenever the carrier already served both endpoint city markets in the prior 12 months. Lagged-persistence baselines are degenerate because every eligible row is a brand-new route, which is why the attrition rate is the persistence stand-in.
task.split_policy: Frozen chronological boundaries by entry month, set before any modelling: train = entries in 2011-01..2014-06; eval (validation) = 2015-10..2016-09; holdout = 2018-01..2018-12. Two 15-month embargo gaps drop all entries in 2014-07..2015-09 and 2016-10..2017-12 so that no split's 14-month label window overlaps the next split's decision period. No entries after 2018-12 are used at all, because their anniversary windows fall inside the COVID-19 schedule collapse and would change the label's meaning. Data pulls cover 2010-01..2020-02 only.
task.target: label = 1 if the carrier's summed DepPerformed (departures performed) on the directed city-market pair over months M+12, M+13 and M+14 equals 0, i.e. the route is not operating at its one-year anniversary; label = 0 if any departures were performed in that three-month anniversary window.
task.usefulness: The label is absent from the entry-month record and requires 15 months of later carrier filings, so the model must predict a forward commercial commitment rather than copy a field. Features are strictly point-in-time and are useful for route development, airport incentive packages and market-entry research. First-month load factor, gauge, competition and whether the carrier opens new stations are informative but not deterministic. The positive rate is measured by the builder rather than assumed.

cross_row_audit.auxiliary_files_review: Only public/train.csv, public/eval.csv and private/holdout.csv are shipped; no fixture labels, target proxies or answer scaffolds are present.
cross_row_audit.rationale: Each scored row carries precomputed point-in-time features; no future or label-derived group rate is shipped.

limitations: No historical vintages or full-row availability ledger are supplied; the current TranStats snapshot is used and training_label_timing is unverified.
No publisher publication schedule was supplied; a conservative 90-day administrative availability lag is assumed for timing metadata and is not a measured publication date.
The source has month-level dates only; the qualification event cluster is the carrier identity, not a day-level event timestamp.
T-100 publication lag is not documented in the supplied evidence; no zero-day publication date is invented.
Absence of a T-100 pair-month row is treated as zero performed departures only after global month coverage and missing-DepPerformed checks; missing feature values are blank rather than zero.
City-market aggregation hides airport-level shifts inside a metro.
Seasonal suspensions, mergers, certificate transfers and carrier re-coding can be coded as route exits.
Entries are not independent within a carrier or hub; route counts overstate independent events.
The frozen population is U.S. certificated carriers and Class F scheduled service; foreign carriers, non-scheduled classes and all-cargo-only service are not described.
Small commuter coverage is uneven and the at-least-8-departures rule removes very thin services.
Entries after 2018-12 are excluded because their anniversary windows cross the 2020 schedule collapse.
The label uses all-class DepPerformed over M+12 through M+14 as frozen; if only scheduled passenger service is intended, the semantics differ.
The base rate is measured by construction and is not assumed.

selection.evidence: Frozen population and split policy; eligibility uses only month M and prior months, while the label uses months M+12 through M+14.
selection.rule: Include one entry episode when Class F, total Passengers greater than zero and total DepPerformed at least 8 in month M, the same carrier has zero performed departures on the directed pair in every month M-12 through M-1, and M falls in a frozen split window. Only month M and prior months enter eligibility or features. Rows whose anniversary window M+12 through M+14 is not fully reported are omitted from supervised output as unknown-label rows and are never labelled negative. No outcome value enters eligibility.

vintage.evidence: Current TranStats bulk files are updated in place; no historical vintage is available in the supplied evidence.

limitations: No licence statement appears on the TranStats download page itself; the public-domain designation is taken from BTS's own data-portal metadata for T-100-derived products plus 17 U.S.C. 105, with BTS requiring source citation. Anyone re-publishing should carry the BTS credit line rather than assert a CC0 dedication over the upstream data.

The download path is an ASP.NET form postback with view-state tokens, not a stable static file URL; eleven annual pulls must be scripted, and the interface could change. The 'Prezipped File' option is the documented fallback.

The label treats a seasonal suspension as an exit whenever the carrier performs no departures in the three-month anniversary window, so genuinely seasonal routes launched in the wrong season are systematically coded as failures.

Corporate events are confounded with route failure: mergers, certificate transfers and UniqueCarrier re-coding make an acquired carrier's routes vanish from the panel and be labelled discontinued even where service continued under another code.

Entry episodes are not independent within carrier or within airport: a carrier that shuts down fails all of its new routes at once, and a hub's entry cohort shares the same local demand shock. Row counts overstate the effective number of independent events.

Domestic U.S. certificated carriers only: foreign-carrier entries, non-scheduled/charter service (classes L/N/P/Q/R/V) and all-cargo-only service are excluded, so results do not describe the whole market.

T-100 coverage of very small commuter operators is uneven and reporting practices vary, which is partly why the >=8 departures-in-entry-month rule is used; that rule also removes genuine but very thin new services.

City-market aggregation deliberately hides airport-level shifts within a metro (e.g. a move from one metro airport to another counts as continuous service), which is a definitional choice, not a measurement of airport-level survival.

All entries after 2018-12 are excluded because their anniversary windows cross the 2020 schedule collapse, so the task describes pre-2019 market structure and is a retrospective, current-vintage construction rather than proof of what an operator could have computed live in 2013.
No performance metrics were computed and none should be inferred from this selection; the base rate and the entry counts above are estimates pending construction.
